claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above approximately 2300 °C to achieve good densification and microstructural integrity.
Earlier ZrB2 specimens processed at approximately 1700 °C were vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
ZrB2 can be adequately densified at 1600–1700 °C in a tailored oxygen-containing or boron-precursor-containing atmosphere.
The tailored sintering atmosphere will induce in situ formation of a nanoscale boron-oxide layer at surfaces and grain boundaries.
A thin, continuous boron-oxide passivation layer can form without disrupting the single-phase ZrB2 bulk microstructure.
Controlled oxygen promotes localized oxidation of boron during sintering.
The localized oxidation produces a thin, adherent oxide layer.
The boron-oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier against further high-temperature oxidation.
The boron-oxide layer acts as a barrier against attack by liquid plating metal.
The tailored processing preserves the mechanical strength of the bulk ZrB2.
Atmosphere-tailored ZrB2 will have greater oxidation durability than conventionally processed approximately 2300 °C ZrB2.
Atmosphere-tailored ZrB2 will have greater liquid-plating-metal corrosion resistance than conventionally processed approximately 2300 °C ZrB2.
Atmosphere-tailored ZrB2 will have greater oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance than earlier low-temperature ZrB2 specimens.
The resulting ceramic will retain mechanical strength and structural integrity comparable to or better than conventional and prior low-temperature ZrB2.
The proposed passivation will remain effective during high-temperature oxidative service.
The proposed passivation will remain effective during exposure to a liquid plating-metal bath.
Variations in atmosphere composition or sintering kinetics may limit reproducibility of the passivation layer.
At least a 20% improvement in both oxidation and corrosion resistance is the proposed quantitative criterion for successful performance.

contradictions.description: The product is repeatedly described as single-phase ZrB2, but the intervention intentionally creates a chemically distinct boron-oxide phase at surfaces and grain boundaries. The bulk may remain ZrB2, but the complete ceramic body would not be strictly single-phase.
